newsitem.title: FRANCE: France delays bailout for Credit Lyonnais.
newsitem.headline: France delays bailout for Credit Lyonnais.

text.p: France announced on Friday it was delaying for more than a month a new rescue plan for Credit Lyonnais in the latest setback to government efforts to put the troubled state-owned bank on its feet.

The surprise decision to postpone the plan, due to be presented this week, came after the European Commission, which must approve state aid packages, sought changes to an outline presented by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis.

A finance ministry spokeswoman said France and the European Commission wanted to limit the amount of public funds poured into the bank, which has already consumed billions of francs in taxpayers' money, and were seeking a fuller rescue plan.
"We agreed to make several adjustments and additions," she said. The decision was made after several conversations this week between Arthuis and the European Commission.

Analysts said they believed the Commission sent the plan back for more details on the cost of the rescue, meant to pave the way for privatisation of Credit Lyonnais. French officials had said earlier this week it was impossible to put a price tag on the package.

The ministry, which threw the bank open to bids last September, also said it now did not expect to be able to sell it for another two years. "We want to have it in shape ready to privatise in two years from now," the spokeswoman said.
Non-voting shares in the bank, which have been on a strong run, closed down 1.16 percent at 196.10 francs.
Once the world's biggest bank outside Japan, Credit Lyonnais was brought near to collapse after a lending spree in the boomtime 1980s backfired and led to massive losses.

European Commission estimates published last December suggested the new aid plan could total some 30 billion francs ($5 billion), not including money to boost the bank's solvency ratios to international levels to make it saleable.

The figures provoked outrage from Credit Lyonnais' private sector rival Societe Generale whiich called for a "controlled liquidation" of the bank, saying taxpayers should not have to foot the bill for its reckless past.
Newspaper reports that the bank could show a big profit recovery in 1997 have further upset its rivals.
Van Miert is believed already to be worried about French bank complaints that the new aid would be a severe distortion in the fiercely competitive financial sector.
Just two years ago, the Commission approved a rescue plan of 45 billion francs in state aid, until then the largest state subsidy it had ever approved.
Credit Lyonnais, which set out to fulfil a Socialist government dream of putting French banking onto the world map, has become a symbol of the worse excesses of the public sector.
Resolving the crisis has forced the government, struggling to ready France for monetary union, to confront Paris's traditional way of doing business in which the state has played a dominant role.
"I hope this revolting experience will pass the message to the nation that the state...should not be a shareholder (in companies)," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said this week.

The government has launched a big programme of privatisations in an attempt to modernise its heavily state-managed economy, but must first inject funds into many state companies to ensure they are saleable.

But in funding Credit Lyonnais and others, it must avoid increasing its budget deficit, which it aims to cut to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year to qualify for European monetary union. In theory, all such funding will come from the government's privatisation revenues.
Under its former chairman, Jean-Yves Haberer, the bank built up a vast array of real estate loans just before the bottom fell out of the French property market in mid-1990.
It lent heavily to businesses which got hammered by the recession, and lent generously abroad, getting burned by, among others, disgraced British newspaper tycoon Robert Maxwell.
It also, via an ill-fated loan to Italian businessman Giancarlo Paretti, became the reluctant owner of Hollywood film studio Metro-Goldwyn Mayer, which it finally sold last year.
